the KSZ in intraplate alkaline magmatism has also been well documented elsewhere [Sykes, 1978]. Such zones of weakness could also act as channels for hydrothermal fluids accompanying the emplacement of the alkaline bodies. The =1100-1050 Ma ages of the Shenango, Nemegosenda, and Lacknet Lake bodies suggest a causal relationship with Keweenawan events in the Lake Superior area immediately to the southwest. Burke and Dewey [1973] proposed that the KSZ was a failed third arm of a Keewenawan triple junction. In fact, the KSZ is a much older structure that has been repeatedly reactivated [Hanes et al., 1992]. In response to the tectonic forces that caused Keweenawan rifting, the KSZ became the site of incipient rifting and alkaline intrusion. The Shenango complex is an elliptical body intruding mafic paragneisses and foliated dioritic rocks. The complex comprises a monzonite core with arcuate mafic hornfels units and a peripheral unit of syenodiorite and diorite on the east side. These units seem to be comagmatic and grade into one other. Unlike other alkaline complexes in the Chapleau block, the Shenango lacks the characteristic units of a carbonatite-alkalic suite and there is no fenitization of the surrounding country rocks. Ours is the first paleomagnetic study of the Shenango body. Samples were taken at eight sims in the northern end of the intrusion, along the railway line and the shore of Shiners Lake. This part of the Shenango intrusion consists of massive fresh diorite with accessory magnetite. Some sites were also taken in the mafic gneiss country rock. The Borden carbonatite is marked by a prominent circular magnetic anomaly with a diameter of 1.6 km. There are no surface outcrops, but exploration trenches and drill holes suggest that the main lithologies are fenire, calcic carbonatite, and silico- carbonatites [Bell et al., 1987]. We sampled two sims for paleomagnetic study in the tonalitic country rock overlying the intrusion. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS We collected an average of six samples per site. Samples were oriented by sun and Brunton compasses. Alternating field (AF) demagnetization in --20 steps to 100 mT and thermal demagnetization in --15 steps, usually to 600øC, were carried out in magnetic shields with standard Schonstedt demagnetizers. The NRM vectors of thermally cleaned specimens were measured with a Schonstedt spinner magnetometer (sensitivity -- 0.05 mA/m). A modified Digico spinner magnetometer with similar sensitivity was used to measure the rest of the specimens. SUMMARY OF PALEOMAGNETIC DATA Using the mean directions (Figure 6) and the location of the site, paleomagnetic poles are calculated for the shale C 1 and C2 directions, the pencil slate direction, and the well-cleaved slate direction (Table 1). Because the dip and strike of the beds throughout the outcrop are fairly uniform, a fold test is not possible. Lacking a traditional paleomagnetic field test to constrain the age of magnetization in the Martinsburg Formation, we include paleopoles using both geographic and stratigraphic coordinates in Table 1. We will attempt to identify the geologically meaningful paleopoles by considering the following: (1) the poles should match other North American poles of Ordovician depositional age or poles with ages of probable remagnetization events and (2) possible structural complexities such as rigid body rotation associated with Pennsylvania salient development, strain alteration of remanence, and synfolding remagnetization.

PALEOMAGNETIC STUDY OF TIlE MARTINSBURG FORMATION Comparison With the North American API We have concluded from magnetite remanence and orientation and from structural geology that the characteristic remanence of the shale is prefolding in age. An independent test of this conclusion can be made by comparing the poles calculated from the characteristic directions of the shale and the reference North American apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Cambrian- Jurassic, generated from the global paleomagnetic data base using all poles from the stable craton with Q_>3 [Van der Voo, 1990] (Figure 12). The tilt-corrected shale C2 pole lies far from any portion of the APWP. This direction is best defined by the Om22A samples in which the remanence is probably carried by pyrrhotite. On this basis we exclude the shale C2 direction from further consideration. The tilt-corrected shale C 1 pole falls near the lower-middle Silurian and lower Devonian portions of the APWP, which would indicate a possible Silurian to lower Devonian remagnetization in the shales. The Nemegosenda carbonatite consists of a nucleus of alkaline syenite and carbonatite, surrounded by brecciated syenitic rocks [Parsons, 1961; Thurston et al., 1977]. Brecciation, alteration, and recrystallization increase outward to a metasomafic aureole. The Archean gneiss in the aureole shows two fenitization zones. The inner zone is characterized by dehydration and reduction with abundant magnetite, and the foliated outer zone is extensively hydrated and oxidized and rich in hematite. Minor late mafic, porphyry, and carbonatite dikes and carbonatite veins occur in and near the complex. Symons and Garber [1974] carried out a paleomagnetic study of 17 sims in different petrological phases in the complex and its aureole. The best section of western Taimyr is situated in the middle Syradasay River, on the left bank on the northern flank of a horst-anticline (72.9”N, 84”E). The regional dip of the lava varies from block to block, from northwest to northeast. Dips change from 70-80” at the bottom of the section to practi- cally horizontal at the top. The entire thickness is about 1.7 km (Fig. 2). The section is subdivided on geochemical grounds, with, from bottom to top, three suites being recog- nised: Syradasaysky, Labaksky and Verhnetamsky. The lavas of the Syradasaysky suite belong to the alkali-basalt series and are represented by trachy- basalts (with Ti-augite), subalkaline basalts with a higher content of olivine, and hawaiites. The silica content of the lower Syradasaysky ‘undersuite’ varies between 44.5 and 48%, whereas that of the hawaiites of the upper undersuite varies between 49.5 and to 52%. These alkali-basalts differ from the overlying tholeiitic basalts by virtue of their 4-6% total con- tent of alkaline elements and owing to the appear- ance of pink Ti-augites. The overlying Labaksky suite is mainly composed of tholeiitic basalts of a more homoge

In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. The demagnetization equipment used was identical in all laboratories. Identical devices and technology have lead to minor scatter of the NRM-component directions isolated by cleaning (see Tables 1-3). Due to the multicomponent behaviour of almost all specimens in the pilot study, eight to 15 demagnetization steps were used for the thermal and AF analysis of interest for all of the remaining specimens. A multicomponent analysis was carried out using Zijderveld diagrams (Zijderveld 1967) and stereoplots (Figs 3-12). A least-squares method was used for calculating NRM-component directions (Kirschvink 1980). The directions, based on three or more points on the diagram, and calculated with an error of 10" or less have been accepted. The polar equi-areal projection was used to plot a distribution of characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions (Figs 13 and 14). The mean directions and Fisher statistics were calculated at the sample level. All ChRM-directional data and rock-magnetic results were collected and analysed in the palaeomagnetic laboratories of VNIGR

In order to improve this situation and to assess the G1 -G5 c 500 0 500m - reliability of the earlier data, a cooperative palaeomagnetic study has been undertaken. Sequences of Lower Proterozoic rocks in the Lake Onega region (both sedimentary and igneous rocks) covering the Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2150 Ma) ages, originally studied by Katzeblin ( 1968), Ignatjeva ( 1974), Khramov & Ignatjeva (1980) and Gooskova & Krasnova (1985), have been resampled. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The sampling region lies close to the west and northwest shore line of Lake Onega, in the southeast Fennoscandian Shield (Fig. 1). This region belongs to the Onega depression, which lies on the southeast side of the Karelian tectonic province (Sokolov 1987). The Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) age sequence comprises two members. The lowest is the Petroz'avodskian Sandstone Formation which has yielded a K-Ar age (on glauconite) of 1800 Ma (Sokolov 1987). Two basaltic lava flows occur in the upper part of this member. The lowest is the Petroz'avodskian Sandstone Formation which has yielded a K-Ar age (on glauconite) of 1800 Ma (Sokolov 1987). Two basaltic lava flows occur in the upper part of this member. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. The peak fields used for the latter two experiments reach 100 mT and 2000 mT respectively. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In the case of stronger remanence, continuous thermal demagnetization was carried out in a thermal demagnetizer incorporated in the spinner magnetometer. Sequences of Lower Proterozoic rocks in the Lake Onega region (both sedimentary and igneous rocks) covering the Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2150 Ma) ages, originally studied by Katzeblin ( 1968), Ignatjeva ( 1974), Khramov & Ignatjeva (1980) and Gooskova & Krasnova (1985), have been resampled. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The sampling region lies close to the west and northwest shore line of Lake Onega, in the southeast Fennoscandian Shield (Fig. 1). This region belongs to the Onega depression, which lies on the southeast side of the Karelian tectonic province (Sokolov 1987). The Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) age sequence comprises two members. The lowest is the Petroz'avodskian Sandstone Formation which has yielded a K-Ar age (on glauconite) of 1800 Ma (Sokolov 1987). Two basaltic lava flows occur in the upper part of this member.
